title.analysis: The title combines a high-arousal adjective with a broad social-comparison target. 'Money stats' accurately signals a statistical roundup, while 'average person' is not a stable denominator: the script switches among full-time workers, consumer units, households, adults, non-retirees, account holders and retirees, and alternates means with medians. The result is therefore well aligned at the category level but methodologically overgeneralized. At 19.76486x against ten frozen peers and 9.52068x against five, it is STRONG in both cohorts; public metadata cannot establish that the wording caused the outlier result.
title.search_demand: Durable self-comparison intent around average income, savings, debt, credit score, spending and net worth. Historical query volume and traffic sources are unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Strong list-level alignment: the transcript covers income, retirement, Social Security, spending, credit, debt, net worth, saving and retirement age. Weak denominator and vintage discipline makes the singular 'average person' promise less precise than the actual evidence.

thumbnail.analysis: The registered 1280x720 image uses oversized black 'WHAT PEOPLE REALLY HAVE' text, a large contemplative cartoon figure, a much smaller worried figure, a thick arrow and a red card displaying 9,000. The headline, arrow and 9,000 amount remain readable at proportional 320x180; the card's tiny currency mark is borderline. The image converts a multi-stat video into one instantly understood reveal and debt-comparison scene, but it does not identify a source, population or date. The $9,000 visual repeats one of the transcript's weakest-denominator claims. Historical upload art, CTR, A/B tests and causal contribution are unavailable.

script.analysis: The script sustains one clear job: help viewers compare their finances with public benchmarks. It defines median, explains net worth, translates annual values into monthly stakes and closes with concrete behaviors. Its main weakness is evidence hygiene. Sources are named generically without table dates, and incompatible populations and measures are presented as one average person. Several figures reproduce exact 2021 or older tables even though newer official data were available by the September 2025 upload. The narrative repeatedly moves from descriptive population statistics to moral judgments about individual discipline, ignoring household composition, housing markets, health, caregiving, unemployment and selection into surveys or accounts. Arithmetic examples generally work, but the sourced inputs and inferences often do not.
claim_audit: STALE/UNDERSTATED: BLS reports $1,204 median weekly earnings for full-time wage and salary workers in 2025, about $62,608 annualized. The script's just-over-$1,000/$52,000 value is not the most recent available benchmark and is not an all-worker average.
UNSUPPORTED RANGE: The claim that $52,000 gross becomes $35,000-$40,000 take-home depends on filing status, state, benefits, credits and deductions; no assumptions are provided.

DENOMINATOR PROBLEM: Federal Reserve SHED data show 28% of non-retired adults had no retirement savings in 2022. That does not mean one quarter of all Americans plans to rely entirely on Social Security. The $65,000 median and age balances are not tied to a specific official table and appear to mix account holders with broader populations.

ARITHMETIC SUPPORTED, RULE CONDITIONAL: Four percent of $88,000 is $3,520 per year, about $293 monthly. The four-percent rule is a planning heuristic with horizon, portfolio and inflation assumptions, not a guaranteed return; Social Security, pensions, work and other assets are excluded.

STALE: SSA reports a $1,975.34 average monthly retired-worker benefit in December 2024. The script's approximately $1,550 value is materially old by the September 2025 publication date. Benefits vary with covered earnings and claiming age.

EXACTLY REPRODUCED BUT STALE: $66,928 total spending, $22,624 housing, $8,289 food and $10,961 transportation are exact BLS 2021 consumer-unit means. They are not current 2025 figures, medians, family-only measures or a required after-tax break-even budget. The script also changes $5,577 to $5,500 in its closing savings example.

SUPPORTED: Experian reports an average FICO score of 715 in Q3 2024. The script's statement that some employers check credit scores is imprecise: employment screening generally uses credit reports, not consumer credit scores, and is subject to law and consent.

UNSUPPORTED/CONFLATED: Experian's Q3 2024 average credit-card balance was $6,730 per consumer with cards, not over $9,000 per household. Household debt, average balance, revolving balance and balance among indebted cardholders are different denominators. Saying most debt bought unnecessary goods is unsupported and ignores emergency or income-shock borrowing.

OUTDATED: The most recent SCF available at publication reported 2022 median family net worth of $192,900 overall and $39,000 for under-35 families. The script's approximately $122,000 and under-$14,000 values correspond to older survey/dollar vintages, yet are called most recent.

MEASURE MISCHARACTERIZED: BEA's personal saving rate is aggregate saving divided by aggregate disposable personal income, not the percent saved by the average person. September 2025 was 4.7%, not 6%; month-to-month revisions and volatility matter.

PARTLY SUPPORTED: Gallup's reported actual retirement age is around 61-62 in recent polls. This is a survey mean among retirees, not administrative evidence that most people choose to stop at 61. Full Social Security retirement age is 67 only for people born in 1960 or later; earlier cohorts have lower full retirement ages.

OVERGENERALIZED: SSA life-expectancy statistics around age 65 support roughly two further decades on average, but averages differ by sex and cohort and do not imply an individual 61-year-old will fund exactly 25 years or remain healthy for a specified span.

UNSUPPORTED CAUSAL/MORAL INFERENCE: Population averages do not establish that the average approach is failing mainly because of weak discipline, nor that saving slightly above an aggregate rate means a viewer is ahead. Income, household composition, benefits, debt cost, emergencies and regional prices materially affect outcomes.

topic.analysis: Broad U.S. personal-finance benchmarking across income, retirement assets, Social Security, spending, credit, revolving debt, net worth, saving and retirement age. The audience problem is uncertainty about whether one's finances are normal. The durable demand is strong, but the evidence requires a denominator-and-date matrix rather than a single average-person story. A defensible version would distinguish person, worker, adult, non-retiree, consumer unit and family; label mean versus median; use the latest publication-time tables; and separate descriptive benchmarks from recommendations.
topic.audience_problem: Viewers want an evidence-based financial baseline but can be misled when unlike populations, means, medians and years are treated as one typical person.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Rebuild as a dated scorecard with one row per measure: source year, population, mean/median, household/person, current value and what it can and cannot tell an individual. Preserve the motivating comparison without calling incompatible aggregates one average person.

virality.analysis: Observed 442,496 frozen views, 8,400 likes and 1,835 comments at 369.5435 days; 19.76486x STRONG against ten same-channel age peers and 9.52068x STRONG against five. It is the largest ratio in its exact pool by a wide margin. The title offers broad identity comparison, the image is extremely legible, and the script supplies many benchmark categories. Those observations do not explain the outlier: impressions, CTR, retention, traffic sources, satisfaction, viewer mix, recommendation exposure and packaging history are unavailable. The same channel's closely related 'Average Net Worth by Age' is only TYPICAL and 'Why Everyone Seems Richer Than You' is WEAK, which is a direct counterexample to a simple social-comparison cause.

original_content_lesson.test: Test a rigorously dated 'What Americans Actually Have in 2025' scorecard against a broad shock package. Put population and median/mean labels on screen, lead with three strongest comparisons, and measure owned CTR, first-source retention and source-link use.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for stored-text coverage, image inspection, arithmetic, source-vintage comparison and cohort reproduction; MEDIUM for topic/package interpretation; LOW for causal performance explanation.
